words: And not that eternal pressure to become like the people who have lost their minds. Yeah. I don't mean insound, I mean senility. How, how would would you feel about living in a, a complex with other people who were retired? You wouldn't like that either? Actually, I don't like people my age en masse. Okay, that's fair. I don't like kids en masse either.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: I like people my age en masse. Yeah, that's right. I like individuals. Oh, just some of my best friends are my age. Yeah. And some of them are quite young. So. I like to be where, where there are a great variety of different ages. It would be very depressing to be in a complex. I think I might feel that way too.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: Let's see. I guess, what else I'd like to ask you is, say, well, one thing we we asked several. Most of the people we interview is the, the Depression and World War Two, what were those. Well. How did they affect you and your family? The depression started us out up there. That's right. Yeah. We, we got back to Ohio somehow, where (unintelligible) and all that.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: I can do that. I think, but, World War Two didn't affect me at all. My husband had been in World War One but that was before I knew him, ten years before I knew him. Yeah. My closest relative in World War One was a second cousin. My brother was too young, he was 13 when it ended. So it didn't have too much. And in World War Two my husband was well past military age.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: He was at the 40s. My son-in-law was the right age, but he was working with (unintelligible) and they couldn't spare him. Yeah. That's, maybe that plutonium was much more important than one more soldier. And I had no sons. So the wars didn't really have any. Personal hurt. Well, how about, then, more recently. What what do you think about this, this era and, and what's going on?

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: It's very interesting. It's a replay of the 20s. I wondered about that. You talked about the intellectualism and. The intellectualism, some of it unrealistic and some of it, a commitment to science. Which we don't have now. This generation seems to be turning away from science into all sorts of irrational creeds. Irrational creeds is a good way to put it.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: Yeah. I don't think we had so much of that. We had more of the, the intellectuals were either following H.L. Mencken and trying to tear down the Victorian structure, which needed tearing down. It got a little too thorough, or they were devoted to science. Do you see. The delinquency is very much the same. We, we were, we were lectured to about the hazards of smoking.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: And since we detected the moralistic tone and there really were no data, we, dismissed it. I didn't smoke, really didn't like it, but, except socially just to prove I could. You were brave. But.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: There was that same pious tone toward smoking that there is now for marijuana. Yeah, yeah. The evidence against tobacco didn't come in for another generation. I don't know what they would (unintelligible) marijuana adventure. So far it's not too damning, but I don't know either. Well, I, do you. And then there was the other, like harder drugs. We had bootleg gin.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: I grew up in Columbus, so only two of us. We didn't get another bootlegger or have a recipe for making it. Is that right? One was this Mary Mercer I mentioned. She had grown up next door to a livery stable that her father, and then she had seen drugs. It was not romantic to really get drunk.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: And I had the beginnings of a thyroid deficiency coming on, so I didn't have enough energy. Yeah, I see. But the others all went in for bootleg liquor, either homemade or bootleg, and sometimes, if it was adulterated with wood alcohol, they got killed. Well, sometimes now your drugs are adulterated with things. The whole thing's a replay. It's so, it must seem so familiar to you.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: Then what do you, what do you see as the outcome in that? Oh, it, Americans have a way of making a pendulum swing. Yeah. It'll swing back, I imagine. Are you, are you at all, you know, do you worry about, say, your daughters and their children? What's. Well, I worry about possible atomic war. Yeah. That's a very real danger and.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: That's. That's not something that one has any control over. Sure, you can't. I think if it starts, it'll start with some crazy man with a bomb. Or some of those little countries getting under control of someone. And now they're. It's possible to, hijack the material. Make your own, isn't it? Yes, yes. With enough (unintelligible). Oh, okay. Well, do you have, do you have anything written down on here that we didn't cover?

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: No, I don't think so. Well, then I guess, I, my, one of my last things I'd like to ask, is there anything that you just feel you'd like to say? Any advice or any feelings that you have about the way your life has been? Remember Robert Frost poem The Path Not Taken? Yeah. I, if I had applied six months sooner, I would have got a job at Stanford, helping Terman with his gifted child study.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: When was this? Well, I just, looked up because I wondered if Melita Oden was the person who got the job I applied for after she got it. She was. Was she? Yes. She's now the senior officer in charge of the Terman study. And I just wonder what it would have been like. I guess so. But.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: I wouldn't have. I wish I could have been twins. So you could do twice as much. Yes. I had intended. A great attitude. I had intended to take the summer off, bat around, be a waitress here and there, that sort of thing, and then go to Stanford that fall. And then I met Bob and that, threw a monkey wrench into that. So that was back in 40, he was, he was 40. He was almost 40, I was almost 30. You were 29. Yes.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: If I hadn't met him, I would eventually have gone to Stanford and it would have been quite different. But I would have missed some very fascinating experiences. I'm not really regretful. I do wish I'd been twins. I want you to tell the title of your book on the tape.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: So we'll know. Oh. This one. Restraints on Excellence. And the subtitle will be Our Waste of Gifted Children. And do you think it will be published in here? Later this spring, I hope. The printer is ready to go, as soon as I get these permissions. When you write to us. And some rewriting. Then, let us know where we can get a copy.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: Because then we can put it in the archives with, with your tape and pictures. Well, I can send you a copy. That'd be just great. I'm selling, I'm selling directly, mostly. Good. Then sell it to the Center. And the Book People in Moscow only charge at 20%. They only benefit 20%. The Book People. That's a good price, I like it. Yes, and the college bookstore here only wants 20%. But the commercial bookstores want 40%.

speaker: Cathy Naugle or Millie (Martha) Burroughs
words: Oh, well. And I expect to lose money on this thing. But I don't want someone else to make quite that much money. Well, this is, this has been so great. I think I've got so much on this tape. What I usually do is go home and listen to them over again and then think about the things I didn't ask.
